analysis.one_liner: Directs the FTC to write rules requiring websites to disclose and let people limit how their personal data is used.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with no cosponsors, it was referred to a House subcommittee and died there without a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required commercial websites to post clear notices about what personal information they collect and how it is used, to give visitors a simple way to consent to or limit the sharing of that information, and to let people find out what data about them was sold or transferred. It would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write and enforce these rules, with state attorneys general also able to sue violators. The bill was introduced on the first day of the 109th Congress, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet users age 13 and older, who would gain notice of data collection, a way to limit disclosure of their information, a means to learn what data about them was sold, and state-level enforcement on their behalf.

how_it_helps.text: Requires commercial websites to post a clear notice identifying the operator, what personal information is collected, how it is used, and what may be shared with other companies.

Requires a meaningful and simple online process for individuals to consent to or limit disclosure of their personal information for unrelated purposes, and lets individuals request a description of what data was sold or transferred and a reasonable means to obtain it.

Requires operators to maintain reasonable procedures protecting the confidentiality, security, and integrity of personal information, enforced by the FTC, with state attorneys general able to sue for damages, restitution, and injunctions on behalf of residents.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial website and online service operators, including online advertisers and data-driven businesses, which would bear the cost of notice, consent, data-access, and security procedures, and would lose unrestricted ability to collect, sell, and share customer data.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes a safe harbor letting operators comply with self-regulatory guidelines written by representatives of the marketing or online industries and approved by the FTC, so industry-written rules could substitute for the mandated protections.
The bill preempts state law where it establishes an inconsistent rule for online privacy, potentially overriding stronger state privacy protections.

Operators would be permitted to terminate service to individuals who refuse to allow further use or collection of their personal information, so opting out could come at the cost of losing access to a service.

The bill carves out broad exceptions: purpose limits do not apply to transactional information or legitimate business uses, and access rights do not cover commercially confidential data obtained from outside sources, among others.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given consumers real notice and control over their personal data at modest compliance cost to website operators, but its design was softened in advance: an industry safe harbor, a federal preemption of state law, and broad exceptions mean the protections were weaker than they first appear. Even so, it would have established, for the first time, a baseline of privacy rights for adults online that did not otherwise exist.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced the first day of the 109th Congress, it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rodney Frelinghuysen introduced the Online Privacy Protection Act of 2005 in the House on January 4, 2005.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on January 4, 2005, and on February 4, 2005 to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection.
No further action was taken; the bill died in subcommittee when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Website operators, online advertisers, and data brokers came out ahead: no federal privacy rules were imposed, and the data-collection economy of the mid-2000s continued unregulated at the federal level. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's death except the status quo of notice-free data collection.

for.name: Rep. Rodney Frelinghuysen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 109th Congress; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 4, 2005 and sent it to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection; never reported the bill or scheduled action on it.

against.name: Rep. Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 109th Congress, never brought the bill to a markup or the floor; the bill's failure to advance sat with his committee's scheduling decisions.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split is recorded; a Republican introduced it alone and no member of either party cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to disclose data practices, offer opt-outs, provide data access, and secure the data they hold, at a cost to their business models built on collecting and using customer information. Its interest ran against the consumers the bill was meant to protect.

Restrictions on collecting, selling, and disclosing personal information would have constrained targeted marketing and data sales. The bill softened this by letting FTC-approved, industry-drafted self-regulatory guidelines serve as a safe harbor from the rules.
